clue.text: Smitten one may be, but, under this, heartbroken

definitions.text: Smitten one may be, but, under this, heartbroken

parts.words: Smitten one may be, but, under this, heartbroken
parts.note: in the Old Testament Joab and Abner smite their victims 'under the rib' numbered five, a blow to the heart; 'smitten' and 'heartbroken' also suggest being lovesick

explanation.surface: A lovesick person is smitten, yet beneath that lies a broken heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The Authorised Version of 2 Samuel repeatedly has men smitten 'under the fifth rib', which lies over the heart, so a blow there is literally heartbreaking.
explanation.definitionFit: The rib numbered five sits over the heart, the spot where biblical killers struck.

clue.text: Man in his first part meets a princess

parts.note: in Shakespeare's 'seven ages of man' speech, the first part a man plays is the baby, 'At first the infant'

explanation.surface: A man in his debut role meets a royal princess.
explanation.walkthrough: As You Like It's 'one man in his time plays many parts'; the first is the infant. 'meets' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish or Portuguese king's daughter is given this title, a princess of the royal house.

clue.text: To Eric the change is academic

indicators.note: a change of the letters to eric the yields a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Whatever happens to Eric, the change is of merely academic interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' belongs to the fodder: all nine letters of TO ERIC THE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something merely academic is theoretical, concerning ideas rather than practice.

clue.text: Saucy, if horsy perhaps-— some might call her a dish

indicators.note: some of the letters of the phrase her a dish are taken, as a run lying within it

explanation.surface: A cheeky, horsey woman whom some men might call a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' and 'horsy' look like a description of a woman, but with 'horse' in front this root makes a sauce. 'some' takes a run from 'her a dish'.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseradish sauce is made from a pungent root, so this root becomes saucy when horsy.

clue.text: The sounds and the result of cooking

definitions.text: The sounds and the result of cooking

parts.words: The sounds and the result of cooking
parts.note: the noises a pan of fried leftovers makes on the stove name the dish itself

explanation.surface: The noises in the kitchen and the meal that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: Fried cabbage and potato bubbles and squeaks as it cooks, and the British dish of leftovers is named after those noises.
explanation.definitionFit: This British fry-up of leftover potato and cabbage is named for the noises it makes in the pan.

clue.text: Ephraim's city is known to Virginian viewers

definitions.meaning: the sanctuary town in the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim where the Ark was kept
the ranch in the TV western The Virginian bore this name

explanation.surface: A biblical town turns out to be familiar to fans of a television western.
explanation.walkthrough: The Virginian was a long-running American TV western set on a Wyoming ranch; 'Virginian' looks like a person from Virginia but names the show.
explanation.definitionFit: One name serves both the Old Testament holy town and the fictional cattle ranch of the western series.

clue.text: Show financial discernment, demanding money down

definitions.meaning: to see or notice money read literally
payment made immediately, in ready cash

explanation.surface: Someone shrewd about finance insists on immediate payment.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first definition as two words: to see where the money is.
explanation.definitionFit: Payment on the nail is known by this term, which taken literally means noticing the money.

clue.text: A boy and a girl for Fidelio

parts.note: Leo is a boy's name
Nora is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Two youngsters cast in Beethoven's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: In Beethoven's opera Fidelio is the disguise of the heroine, who poses as a young man to rescue her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's heroine takes the alias Fidelio while disguised as a prison assistant.

clue.text: One Peggotty presented a clumsy appearance

parts.note: Ham Peggotty is the fisherman nephew in Dickens's David Copperfield
to have handed something over is to have presented it

explanation.surface: A Dickens character cutting an awkward figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The Peggotty family in David Copperfield include Clara, Daniel and the nephew Ham.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ham-fisted handles things awkwardly, the same as clumsy.

clue.text: Transgress, like farmer's wife attacking mouse ?

definitions.meaning: to sin or commit a wrong
in the nursery rhyme Three Blind Mice the farmer's wife cuts their tails off with a carving knife, so the rear part comes away

explanation.surface: Someone does wrong in the manner of the nursery-rhyme woman with the carving knife.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second definition as two words: the farmer's wife takes the tail end clean away from each mouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To give moral offence is to sin; read as a phrase it describes a tail lopped away.

clue.text: A voracious reader

parts.note: both a person who devours volumes and a grub that literally eats through bindings and pages

explanation.surface: A description of someone who reads constantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voracious' is literal for the insect larva that bores through old volumes, and figurative for the keen human reader.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect larva that eats paper gives its name to people who read incessantly.

clue.text: Ten madly backing loser " Mezzanine "

indicators.note: acting madly the three letters of the word ten get jumbled into a new order
backing means the word loser is written from its last letter to its first

explanation.surface: Ten wildly supporting a failure in some theatre's mezzanine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' turns TEN into ENT; 'backing' turns LOSER into RESOL; together they give the French word for a mezzanine floor.
explanation.definitionFit: An entresol is a low storey between ground and first floor, the same thing as a mezzanine.

clue.text: Smoke in sunny environment

definitions.meaning: a smoke is a cigar, and a large straight-sided Havana bears this name
the halo of plasma surrounding the sun, seen during an eclipse

explanation.surface: Smoke drifting in sunny surroundings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a long cigar and the glowing outer atmosphere around the sun.

clue.text: A sticker, but not a girl's best friend

definitions.meaning: an adhesive such as wallpaper glue
diamonds are a girl's best friend, and imitation gems are made of glass called by this name

explanation.surface: A label that, unlike diamonds, is no girl's best friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The song says diamonds are a girl's best friend; the clue points to fake gemstones of lead glass, which share the name of glue.
explanation.definitionFit: Glue for wallpaper and glass imitation jewellery share this word.

clue.text: Fantastic notion to switch from cigarettes?

definitions.text: Fantastic notion to switch from cigarettes?

parts.words: Fantastic notion to switch from cigarettes?
parts.note: an unrealistic hope, originally the fancy of an opium smoker, read literally as a dream about a different kind of smoke

explanation.surface: A far-fetched idea about giving up cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for an impossible hope comes from opium smokers' visions; the question mark flags the literal reading of a smoker dreaming of a briar.
explanation.definitionFit: An unrealistic hope or fantasy, from opium smokers' visions.

clue.text: Was it wandering musicians told to belt up hereabouts ?

indicators.note: the letters of was it wander out of place and settle in a new arrangement

parts.note: a group of musicians is a band

explanation.surface: Travelling players being told to keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering' turns WAS IT into WAIST. 'Belt up' looks like the British slang for 'be quiet' but is literal: this is where a belt is fastened.
explanation.definitionFit: The strip at the top of trousers or a skirt is where one fastens a belt.

clue.text: Q.C. academician takes up a French nobleman to fish

parts.note: a Queen's Counsel is a senior barrister, a member of the profession called the Bar
RA stands for Royal Academician

indicators.note: in a down clue taking up means lifting the words upward, so they read backwards

parts.note: a duc is a French duke

explanation.surface: A senior lawyer and an artist pick up a French duke on the way to go fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes up' reverses A DUC into CUDA, which follows BAR and RA.
explanation.definitionFit: A large predatory tropical sea creature with fearsome teeth.

clue.text: Providing you get car in for repair

indicators.note: sent for repair, the letters of get car in are taken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A garage promise: provided you bring the car in, it gets fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Providing' looks like 'provided that', but it means supplying food.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplying food and drink for events is catering, i.e. providing.

clue.text: Good money Somerset town's got for fish

parts.note: pi is short for pious, so it means good
L is the abbreviation for a pound, the British money unit
Chard is a market town in Somerset, England, and its possessive supplies a final S

explanation.surface: Someone receives good money from a Somerset town in exchange for fish.
explanation.walkthrough: PI (pious) and L (pound, from Latin libra) are crossword standards; CHARD is a small town in the county of Somerset in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: These small oily fish of the herring family are adult sardines.

clue.text: Understand Jenny's outside, with this poultice

indicators.note: Lind is placed outside, with its letters wrapped around the other piece

parts.note: Jenny Lind was a famous nineteenth-century Swedish soprano
to see is to understand

explanation.surface: Grasping that Jenny is out there, with a soothing poultice.
explanation.walkthrough: Jenny Lind, 'the Swedish Nightingale', was a soprano famous in Victorian Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Crushed flaxseed was the classic base for a hot poultice.

clue.text: Free fare for circus-goers

parts.note: the Roman poet Juvenal said the populace wanted only '... and circuses', the food handed out to crowds at the games

explanation.surface: A free meal for people going to the circus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circus' here is the ancient Roman arena: emperors kept the mob content with free grain and games.
explanation.definitionFit: Juvenal's phrase panem et circenses pairs free food with public games in the arena.

clue.text: Movement to go French and English with some overlapping

indicators.note: with some overlapping says the end of the French verb slides over into the English word

parts.note: aller is the French verb 'to go'
the English for 'to go' is go

explanation.surface: Instructions to leave in two languages that partly overlap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with some overlapping' moves the R of ALLER past the G into GO, interleaving the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast section of a symphony or sonata is often marked with this tempo word, so it names a movement.

clue.text: Mammy's boy, million mile walker

definitions.meaning: the blackface singer famous for the song 'My Mammy'
the same singer's song 'I'd walk a million miles for one of your smiles'

explanation.surface: A mother's boy who walks enormous distances.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Jolson starred in The Jazz Singer and sang 'My Mammy', whose lyrics include walking a million miles.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases point to Al Jolson's signature song about his mother and the miles he would walk for her.

clue.text: Many fish do when strung up

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number, so it stands for many
to fish with rod and line is to angle

explanation.surface: Lots of fish hang from a line once caught and strung up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fish' looks like a noun in the surface but is the verb 'angle'; 'Many' is a crossword convention for a large Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Things hung up by a cord swing loosely, which is what this verb describes.

clue.text: Whither Mensa, in translation? (You can say that again !)

parts.note: quo is Latin for 'whither', to where
mensa is the Latin word meaning table, the first noun learnt in Latin grammar; 'in translation' links the two

explanation.surface: Puzzling over the Latin question of where Mensa goes, with an aside agreeing loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are Latin turned into English: QUO is 'whither' and mensa is 'table', the word every Latin primer begins with. 'in translation' only tells you to translate.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark worth repeating is one people will cite; 'You can say that again' captures that.

clue.text: School task will benefit the sedentary

definitions.meaning: a set piece of homework or practice in class
physical activity is what people who sit all day need

explanation.surface: Homework that would do inactive people some good.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a practice task set in class and bodily training for fitness.

clue.text: Pride came before this plant historically

definitions.text: Pride came before this plant historically

parts.words: Pride came before this plant historically
parts.note: pride comes before a fall, but in 1648 Colonel Pride expelled members from Parliament in an event named after him; joining his possessive S to the event gives the plant

explanation.surface: Pride came before a fall, the proverb says, and before this plant in history.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb suggests 'fall'; instead think of Pride's Purge, when Colonel Thomas Pride barred MPs from the English Parliament in 1648: 'Pride' plus the S and the event's second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphorbia, a family of plants with milky sap, has this common name.

clue.text: St. Joan's English soldier turns into a wild beast

indicators.note: turns means the soldier's nickname is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: Joan of Arc and the French called English soldiers 'goddams' after their favourite oath

explanation.surface: An English soldier in Joan of Arc's story becomes a savage animal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shaw's Saint Joan the English are 'goddams', from their swearing; 'turns' reverses that nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabid or vicious dog is a wild and dangerous animal.

clue.text: Jumper, pocket-size originally

parts.note: a jumper is a leaping animal, and the marsupial's baby begins life tiny enough to live in its mother's pouch

explanation.surface: A sweater that started out small enough to fit a pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like the British word for a sweater, but it is a leaping animal; its young start out small enough to fit in a pouch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian marsupial hops and carries its newborn, barely an inch long, in a pouch.
